Microbial Dynamics during the Removal of Linear
Alkylbenzenesulfonate (LAS) under Anaerobic and Microaerobic
Conditions with Different Co-substrates
Maurício Guimarães de Oliveira, Vicente Elício Porfiro Sales Gonçalves da Silva,
Amanda de Sousa e Silva, Fabricio Motteran, and André Bezerra dos Santos*

ABSTRACT: Linear alkylbenzenesulfonate (LAS) is the most
widely used anionic surfactant and is commonly found in
wastewater due to its extensive use in detergents and cleaning
products. Although LAS is biodegradable, its degradation in
anaerobic environments remains a challenge, often requiring the
addition of co-substrates and optimized operating conditions. This
pioneering study evaluates the microbiological pathways and
metabolisms underlying LAS biodegradation in UASB reactors
operated under microaerated conditions, compared with strictly
anaerobic systems. Furthermore, the effects of different co-
substrates (ethanol and sucrose) on LAS removal efficiency and
biogas production were also evaluated. The results indicate that
microaeration, combined with sucrose as a co-substrate, significantly improves LAS removal, increasing efficiency by 34.3%. The
study also revealed that microaeration influenced methane production, reducing its purity but increasing overall volumetric biogas
production. Microaeration significantly influenced the microbial structure and function of the systems, depending on the co-
substrate used. In the presence of ethanol, both systems showed a predominance of fermentative and methanogenic communities,
with no significant differences in LAS removal. In contrast, with sucrose, microaeration promoted greater removal efficiency,
associated with the selection of a specialized consortium composed of Pleomorphomonas and Desulfovibrio, capable of partially
oxidizing the benzene ring and desulfonating the surfactant. This condition activated oxidative and sulfur metabolism pathways,
while maintaining functional methanogenesis, resulting in a less diverse but metabolically more targeted and efficient community in
LAS degradation. These findings highlight the potential of microaeration and co-substrate selection to optimize anaerobic treatment
of LAS-containing wastewater while maintaining stable reactor performance.
1. INTRODUCTION
Upflow Anaerobic Sludge Blanket (UASB) reactors are widely
applied for domestic wastewater treatment and have
increasingly been investigated for the removal of emerging
contaminants (ECs), which are of concern due to their
persistence and ecotoxicological effects.1−3 Among them,
Linear Alkylbenzenesulfonate (LAS) is the most extensively
used anionic surfactant worldwide and is frequently detected in
domestic wastewater because of its widespread use in
detergents, cleaning products, and personal care formula-
tions.4,5 LAS concentrations in wastewater treatment plant
influents typically range from 0.8 to 21 mg·L−1,6 and its
occurrence in aquatic environments has been associated with
foam formation, reduced oxygen transfer, and diminished light
penetration.4,7
Although LAS can be removed under anaerobic conditions,
with efficiencies in UASB reactors ranging between 30% and
91%, its biodegradation remains highly dependent on electron
donor availability and the activity of specialized microbial
consortia, which partly explains the large variability in removal
efficiencies reported for UASB reactors.5,7−9 In this context,
readily fermentable co-substrates such as ethanol and sucrose
can enhance LAS removal by supplying reducing equivalents
and metabolic intermediates that sustain syntrophic inter-
actions and support co-metabolic degradation processes.2,6
The importance of these interactions stems from the fact
that anaerobic LAS biodegradation is inherently more complex
than its aerobic counterpart, as it relies on energetically less
favorable pathways involving fumarate addition to the alkyl
chain, followed by β-oxidation, aromatic ring cleavage, and

desulfonation.10 Consequently, the complete transformation of
LAS depends on the coordinated activity of multiple microbial
populations, including members of the Synergistetes phylum as
well as genera such as Pseudomonas and Desulfovibrio, which
have frequently been associated with the degradation of
aromatic and sulfonated intermediates in anaerobic environ-
ments.6,11,12 As a result, limitations in electron transfer,
syntrophic cooperation, and the activation of key degradation
steps often restrict LAS biodegradation under strictly anaerobic
conditions.
Despite the growing number of studies investigating LAS
degradation in anaerobic reactors, most efforts have focused on
reactor configuration, hydraulic retention time, biomass
adaptation, and the use of supplementary carbon sources.
These studies have demonstrated that LAS removal can be
achieved under anaerobic conditions, but the reported
efficiencies remain highly variable and frequently limited by
the slow degradation of aromatic intermediates, insufficient
electron transfer, and the accumulation of partially transformed
metabolites. Consequently, strategies capable of overcoming
these biochemical bottlenecks while preserving the energetic
advantages of anaerobic treatment remain an important
research challenge.
Given that LAS degradation is typically more efficient under
aerobic conditions, the strategic introduction of low-oxygen
doses into anaerobic systems via microaeration emerges as a
promising approach to enhance surfactant removal. Controlled
microaerobic inputs can stimulate facultative and micro-
aerotolerant microbial taxa, promote the partial oxidation of
xenobiotic intermediates, and facilitate subsequent anaerobic
transformations, all while preserving the redox conditions
required for stable methanogenesis and biogas production.13
Microaeration has consistently enhanced the removal of
diverse recalcitrant pollutants. For BTEX compounds,
microaeration rates of 0.5−2.0 mL air·min−1 increased overall
removal to above 83%, with benzene elimination rising by
approximately 30% relative to anaerobic conditions.14 In the
case of pharmaceuticals, applying microaeration in an
Anaerobic Biofilm Blanket −Membrane Bioreactor system
increased antibiotic degradation to 78% for ciprofloxacin and
88−91% for sulfamethoxazole, clearly surpassing the non-
aerated reactor.15 For dyes, microaeration enabled the
complete removal of aromatic amines from the dye DB22 in
a UASB reactor, producing an effluent 16 times less toxic than
that from the anaerobic control.16 Similarly, for hormones and
pharmaceuticals, an airflow of 4 mL·min−1 increased removal
to 90−94%, compared to less than 30% under strictly
anaerobic operation.17 Microaeration is also widely applied
for hydrogen sulfide oxidation in biogas treatment.18
Collectively, these studies indicate that microaeration acts as
a process intensification strategy capable of selectively
activating oxygen-dependent reactions that are inaccessible
under strictly anaerobic conditions. By modifying local redox
conditions, controlled oxygen supply can influence microbial
community structure, extracellular polymeric substances
production, and the distribution of metabolic functions
responsible for contaminant transformation.19−21 Conse-
quently, oxygen availability not only affects the overall extent
of LAS removal, but also determines the dominant
biodegradation routes involved in its mineralization. Recent
studies have demonstrated that variations in oxygen supply can
shift the balance between aerobic and anaerobic metabolic
pathways, alter the abundance of key functional micro-
organisms, and modify the fate of LAS transformation
intermediates.22,23 Together, these findings highlight that
oxygen acts not merely as an electron acceptor, but as a key
regulator of the biological processes governing LAS degrada-
tion. Nevertheless, despite these advances, the application of
controlled oxygen supplementation for LAS removal in
anaerobic reactors remains unexplored.
In addition, previous studies have shown that LAS
degradation is strongly influenced by operational parameters
that regulate microbial metabolism, including oxygen avail-
ability, nutrient balance, electron donor supply, and microbial
community composition.20,23,24 Variations in these factors can
substantially modify degradation pathways, extracellular
polymeric substances accumulation, nitrogen transformation
routes, and the abundance of key microbial populations
involved in LAS mineralization.20,24 Although co-substrate
supplementation and microaeration have independently been
shown to enhance the biodegradation of recalcitrant
compounds, their combined effects on anaerobic LAS removal
remain unknown. This knowledge gap is particularly relevant
because oxygen supplementation and co-substrate availability
simultaneously affect electron transfer, syntrophic interactions,
oxidative activation reactions, and microbial adaptation to
surfactant stress, all of which are key processes governing LAS
transformation.
Therefore, this study evaluated the combined influence of
controlled microaeration and readily degradable co-substrates
on LAS removal in UASB reactors treating synthetic domestic
wastewater. Particular attention was given to understanding
whether oxygen supplementation could overcome metabolic
bottlenecks traditionally associated with anaerobic LAS
degradation and whether the nature of the co-substrate
influences this response. In addition to reactor performance,
the metabolic pathways potentially involved in LAS trans-
formation were investigated to provide a mechanistic
interpretation of the observed behavior.
2. MATERIALS AND METHODS
The present study was structured into two distinct experiments. The
first experiment involved the continuous operation of two reactors to
evaluate the effects of microaeration and the use of different co-
substrates (ethanol and sucrose) on LAS removal. The second
experiment consisted of a batch assay designed to preliminarily assess
the role of primary fermentative microorganisms (represented by
sucrose), secondary fermentative microorganisms (represented by
ethanol), and acetoclastic methanogenic archaea (represented by
acetate), as well as abiotic and endogenous processes, in relation to
LAS removal efficiencies in continuous-flow experiments under the
tested operational conditions.
2.1. Continuous Operation Experiment Setup
Two cylindrical acrylic UASB reactors (Figure S1) were operated in
parallel at the laboratory scale, with a working volume of 3.25 L. Both
reactors were inoculated with 1.6 L of sludge and operated under the
same conditions, differing only in the microaeration insert: R1,
traditional UASB, R2, microaerated UASB (renamed to UMSB −
Upflow Microaerobic Sludge Blanket).
The inoculum was sludge from a UASB reactor treating sewage in
Caucaia, Brazil. Total solids, total volatile solids and total fixed solids
in the inoculum sludge were 48 ± 3, 25 ± 1, and 23 ± 1 g·L−1,
respectively.
Microaeration in R2 was performed with synthetic air (80%
N2:20% O2, White Martins, Brazil) at its base using a mass flow
controller (GFC17, Cole-Parmer, USA). The microaeration air dose
used in R2 was approximately 0.7 Lair·min−1, corresponding to 0.1

The experiment was conducted in two sequential phases, each

first phase, ethanol was used as the co-substrate, and in the second
phase, sucrose was introduced to evaluate its impact on system
performance. During the stabilization interval, the reactors were fed
with ethanol in the absence of LAS to reset microbial activity and
ensure a clear transition between phases. This structured approach
allowed for a systematic comparison of the effects of different co-
substrates on organic matter degradation and LAS removal under
both anaerobic and microaerobic conditions.
2.2. Batch Experiment
At the end of the first operational phase, sludge samples from both
reactors were collected, homogenized, and used in the presence of
acetate, ethanol, and sucrose to assess LAS degradation and
methanogenesis. The experiment was conducted in triplicate,
following the methodology described by Angelidaki et al.26 Anaerobic
reactors consisted of 300 mL borosilicate glass flasks with a working
volume of 200 mL and a 100 mL headspace, maintained under
continuous agitation at 150 rpm and 35 ± 1 °C.
A substrate-to-microorganism ratio (S/M) of 0.5 gCOD·gVS−1 was
adopted, based on a final concentration of 1 gCOD·L−1 for the
substrate and 2.0 gVS·L−1 for the inoculated sludge. The basal
medium included LAS (15 mg·L−1), macro- and micronutrients, and
sodium bicarbonate (1 g·L−1) as a buffering agent. Two control
groups were established: (i) endogenous control (containing LAS,
sludge, and basal medium, but no additional carbon source), and (ii)
chemical control (containing only LAS and distilled water), as
illustrated in Figure S2.
All reactors were sealed with butyl rubber stoppers and purged with
nitrogen (N2) for approximately 1 min to ensure anaerobic
conditions. The experiment was conducted over 174 h, a period
determined based on the cessation of CH4 production, indicating the
completion of the anaerobic digestion process in batch mode.
2.3. Synthetic Wastewater
The synthetic wastewater consisted of an aqueous solution containing
LAS (15 mg·L−1), ethanol (1 gCOD.L−1) (Phase I), sucrose (1
gCOD.L−1) (Phase II), basal medium (macro and micronutrients)
prepared according to Firmino et al.27 and sodium bicarbonate (1 g·
L−1) to maintain the pH close to 7.0. All reagents were used as
purchased without further purification. The synthetic influent was
kept refrigerated at 4 °C to prevent natural biodegradation of organic
matter.
2.4. Chemical Analysis
Chemical oxygen demand (COD), pH, total suspended solids, and
total solids content were determined according to APHA.28 The
quantification of CH4, CO2, H2, and H2S in the biogas was
determined by gas chromatography with ionization detection by
dielectric barrier discharge (GC BID-2010 Plus, Shimadzu Corpo-
ration, Japan), equipped with GS-GASPRO column (60 m × 0.32
mm) (Agilent Technologies Inc., USA). Helium gas was used as the
carrier gas (White Martins LTDA, Brazil) at a flow rate of 2 mL·
min−1, with a run time of 9 min. Oven, injector, and detector
temperatures were 50, 100, and 250 °C, respectively. O2 and N2 were
quantified by gas chromatography with thermal conductivity detection
(GC-TCD) (GC-17A, Shimadzu Corporation, Japan). The biogas
sample (1.0 mL) was injected in splitless mode, and chromatographic
separation was performed on a Mol Sieve 5A PLOT column (30 m,
0.32 mm ID) (Restek Corporation, USA). Oven, injector, and
detector temperatures were 35, 40, and 230 °C, respectively. Helium
(White Martins LTDA, Brazil) was used as the carrier gas at a flow
rate of 7 mL·min−1, and the run time was 5 min.
LAS concentrations were determined according to the method-
ology adapted from Silva et al.29 by high-performance liquid
chromatography (HPLC) using a Shimadzu system (CBM-20A,
SPD-20A, CTO-20A, SIL-20A, and LC-20AT) equipped with a
reversed-phase C18 column from Shimadzu. The mobile phase was
water with 5 mmol·L−1 ammonium acetate (solvent A) and
acetonitrile (solvent B); the mobile phase flow rate was 1 mL·
min−1, the sample volume was 50 μL, the temperature of the
thermostated column compartment was 40 °C, and UV-Vis detection
at 230 nm. A gradient was applied to the mobile phase to separate the

2.5. Microbiological Analysis
At the beginning of the experiment and the end of each phase, sludge
samples from both reactors were collected to analyze the microbial
changes. For this purpose, sludge samples were collected from
different reactors’ heights, characterizing a biomass composite sample.
0.25 g of fresh sample (total wet weight) was used to extract DNA
from microorganisms using the PowerSoil® DNA Isolation Kit
(QIAGEN, Hilden, Alemanha), following the manufacturer’s
instructions. Based on the V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene, amplicon
sequencing was performed in triplicate according to the Illumina
protocol, using specific primers (515F/806R).30,31
After indexing, the PCR products (amplicons) were purified using
Agencourt AMPure XP-PCR purification beads (Beckman Coulter,
Fisher Scientific, USA), according to the product manual, and
quantified using the dsDNA BR assay kit (Invitrogen, ThermoFisher
Scientific, USA) on a Qubit 2.0 fluorimeter (Invitrogen, Thermo-
Fisher Scientific, USA). The amplicons were sequenced using the
MiSeq 300-cycle chemistry reagent kit (Illumina, USA) on the MiSeq
desktop sequencer (Illumina, USA) at the Genomics and
Bioinformatics Center (CeGenBio) at UFC.
The sequencing data were analyzed using bioinformatics tools. The
DADA2 package v1.28.032 was used to filter and assemble reads into
amplicon sequence variants (ASVs). The obtained sequences were
taxonomically classified using version 5.1 of the MiDAS database,
which catalogs microorganisms identified in anaerobic digesters, with
the assign Taxonomy method of the DADA2 package. Alpha diversity
indices were estimated with the estimate_richness method of the
Phyloseq package v1.44.0. The raw sequence data obtained in this
study have been deposited in the National Center for Biotechnology
Information (NCBI) BioProject database, ID PRJNA836880.
To infer the metabolic capabilities of the microbial communities
present in the reactors samples, the ASV-based 16S rRNA abundance
data were analyzed using PICRUSt2 (Phylogenetic Investigation of
Communities by Reconstruction of Unobserved States). Functional
predictions were generated based on KEGG (Kyoto Encyclopedia of
Genes and Genomes) pathways, using EC (Enzyme Commission)
numbers and KO (KEGG Orthology) identifiers to assign putative
gene functions.33−36

2.6. Statistical Methods
The Mann−Whitney nonparametric test, which do not require
specific distributional assumptions, were used to compare reactor
performance across the different experimental periods at the 5%
significance level (p < 0.05).
3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
3.1. Linear Alkylbenzenesulfonate (LAS) Removal
To evaluate the effects of co-substrate type and microaeration
on reactor performance, LAS removal was monitored during
both the acclimatization and stability phases (Figure 1).
During acclimatization, all reactors exhibited considerable
variability, with standard deviations exceeding 10% of the
mean removal efficiency, indicating that the microbial
communities were still adapting to the operational conditions.
In contrast, LAS removal became more stable after reactor
stabilization, particularly in the sucrose-fed systems, reflecting
the establishment of a more robust microbial consortium.
During the stability period under ethanol feeding, LAS
removal averaged 19.2 ± 3.2% in the control reactor (R1) and
20.8 ± 4.1% in the microaerated reactor (R2), with no
statistically significant difference between reactors (p = 0.32).
When sucrose replaced ethanol as the co-substrate, LAS
removal increased significantly in both systems. In R1, removal
efficiency increased from 19.2 to 25.8% (p = 0.034), whereas in
R2 it increased from 20.8 to 34.3% (p < 0.001). The highest
removal efficiency was therefore achieved by the combination
of microaeration and sucrose supplementation, suggesting a
synergistic effect between oxygen availability and co-substrate
composition.
These findings indicate that co-substrate selection exerted a
greater influence on LAS degradation than microaeration
alone. Sucrose, as a readily fermentable carbohydrate, likely
promoted faster production of volatile fatty acids and
supported a broader range of fermentative, facultative, and
syntrophic microorganisms, creating metabolic conditions
more favorable for surfactant biodegradation than those
established with ethanol.37,38 The effect was particularly
evident under microaerated conditions, where the enhanced
metabolic flexibility may have facilitated the coexistence of
oxidative and anaerobic pathways potentially involved in LAS
degradation.
The LAS removal efficiencies obtained under ethanol
feeding were higher than those reported by Okada et al.,8
who achieved 9.0 ± 2.4% removal in UASB reactors operated
under comparable LAS concentrations using a co-substrate
mixture of ethanol, methanol, and yeast extract. Moreover,
although the same authors observed that increasing co-
substrate complexity enhanced LAS removal, reaching up to
50% with yeast extract supplementation, the present study
demonstrates that sucrose alone was sufficient to significantly
improve LAS degradation under shorter hydraulic retention
time conditions (8 h). These observations reinforce the
importance of co-substrate characteristics in determining the
metabolic potential of anaerobic communities involved in LAS
degradation.
In contrast, Macedo et al.39 reported higher LAS removal
with ethanol than with a sucrose−ethanol mixture in a
fluidized-bed reactor. This discrepancy is likely related to
differences in reactor configuration and operating conditions,
highlighting that the effect of co-substrate selection depends on
the operational environment.
From a practical perspective, the superior performance
achieved by the microaerated reactor supplemented with
sucrose demonstrates the potential of combining low-intensity
oxygen supply with an appropriate co-substrate as a process
intensification strategy for UASB reactors treating LAS-
containing domestic wastewater. Because the improvement
was obtained under an HRT of 8 h, a hydraulic condition
compatible with full-scale domestic wastewater treatment
plants, this approach may enhance LAS removal without
requiring larger reactor volumes or major modifications to
conventional UASB operation.
3.2. Volumetric Biogas Production
To investigate the effects of co-substrate type and microaera-
tion on methane generation, volumetric biogas production and
methane content were evaluated. Figure 2 shows volumetric
biogas and methane production in reactors operated with
sucrose and ethanol as substrates. Monitoring data show that
both reactors achieved higher volumetric methane production
with sucrose. Under ethanol feeding, R1 (conventional UASB
reactor) produced an average of 1.8 ± 0.4 L·day−1, whereas the
microaerated reactor (R2) reached 2.7 ± 0.5 L·day−1. With
sucrose, both reactors showed similar performance: R1 yielded
2.7 ± 0.3 L·day−1, and R2 achieved 2.7 ± 0.4 L·day−1. These
findings indicate that sucrose, as a more complex substrate,
supported more uniform methane production across config-
urations.
Sucrose, a disaccharide composed of glucose and fructose, is
hydrolyzed by hydrolytic bacteria into readily fermentable
monosaccharides. These are processed through glycolysis into
organic acids, which are subsequently transformed into acetate
and methane by acetoclastic methanogens.38 Additionally,
monosaccharides are converted into hydrogen (H2) and
carbon dioxide (CO2), which hydrogenotrophic methanogens
further reduce to methane. Ethanol, in contrast, undergoes a
narrower metabolic route, being directly oxidized into acetate
or H2 + CO2 by acetogenic bacteria prior to methanogenesis.40
Average methane concentration in biogas produced by R1
reached 73.9% during ethanol and 73.4% during sucrose
operation, values exceeding the typical range for conventional
anaerobic digestion (50−70%),5 reflecting the absence of
oxygen and the dominance of methanogenic activity.
In contrast, microaerated systems showed lower methane
content, averaging 36.6% (ethanol) and 32.7% (sucrose). For
biogas to be considered a suitable energy source, the methane
concentration must exceed 45%.41 This reduction is primarily
due to dilution from air injection, along with possible shifts in
microbial community structure induced by oxygen.
These trends were consistent with findings by Nascimento et
al.17 and Oliveira et al.,42 who reported that microaeration
enhances organic matter removal but compromises methane
purity. Because the lower methane concentration mainly
resulted from biogas dilution rather than inhibition of
methanogenic activity, strategies such as controlled oxygen
dosing, intermittent microaeration, or oxygen-enriched streams
may reduce this effect while preserving the oxidative
microzones required for LAS transformation and the energetic
advantage of anaerobic treatment.
3.3. Batch Experiment
A batch experiment was conducted under anaerobic conditions
to preliminarily assess the role of primary fermentative
microorganisms (represented by sucrose), secondary fermen-
tative microorganisms (represented by ethanol), and aceto-

Endogenous controls revealed that 20% of LAS was

Therefore, LAS removal was attributed to biological processes,

LAS removal efficiencies from the liquid phase after 174 h of

and 59.1 ± 3.2% for the sucrose, ethanol, acetate, and

which lacked both co-substrate and biomass, indicating that
LAS is not self-biodegradable under the conditions tested.
LAS removal rates were 0.26 ± 0.4 mg·L−1·h−1 (sucrose),
0.16 ± 0.2 mg·L−1·h−1 (ethanol), 0.18 ± 0.3 mg·L−1·h−1
(acetate), and 0.16 ± 0.2 mg·L−1·h−1 (endogenous). These
results suggest that co-substrates influence the assimilation rate
of organic matter, with sucrose supporting higher LAS
degradation rates than the other conditions, including the
endogenous control.
Among the tested co-substrates, the acetate series exhibited
the lowest LAS removal efficiency. This may be attributed to
the metabolic limitations or sensitivity of microorganisms,
particularly acetoclastic methanogens, to the anionic surfac-
tant.6 Granatto et al.43 also noted that acetoclastic metha-
nogens are more susceptible to surfactant toxicity, whereas
hydrogenotrophic archaea are generally more resilient.
An important point to note was the high LAS removal
observed in the endogenous control, indicating that in the
absence of more efficient substrates for co-metabolic processes,
such as sucrose or ethanol, LAS may be directly utilized by the
microorganisms present or degraded through alternative co-
metabolic pathways involving exopolysaccharides or substrates
derived from endogenous metabolism.
3.4. Molecular Biology
3.4.1. Microbial Community Richness and Diversity.
To evaluate how co-substrate type and microaeration affected
microbial richness and diversity, alpha-diversity indices and
ASV distribution were analyzed. In general, although richness
and diversity indices were higher in the Bacteria domain, they
showed distinct behaviors within the Archaea (Figure 3a) and
Bacteria (Figure 3b) domains, modulated by the nature of the
co-substrate and the presence of residual oxygen introduced in
R2.

across all co-substrates. The conventional reactor (R1) showed

greater richness and diversity, suggesting a more complex and
balanced methanogenic community under strictly anaerobic
conditions. The greater diversity of archaea in R1 may be
associated with greater functional redundancy and trophic
stability typical of consolidated anaerobic systems, but did not
necessarily reflect greater efficiency in LAS degradation. This is
because methanogenic archaea, although essential in the final
stage of anaerobic digestion, predominantly convert simple
intermediates into methane and do not directly participate in
the oxidative reactions involved in LAS breakdown.8,43
In the bacterial domain, however, the response was more
sensitive to the type of co-substrate. When ethanol was used,
the microaerated reactor (R2) showed greater bacterial
richness and diversity, indicating that the controlled oxygen
availability favored the growth of facultative and micro-
aerophilic groups that could coexist with strict anaerobes.
This increased diversity may have broadened the system’s
metabolic spectrum, although, in this case, LAS removal did
not show a statistically significant difference between the
reactors. This result suggests that, under ethanol, LAS
degradation occurred mainly through anaerobic mechanisms,
dependent on specific consortia already well adapted to the
surfactant, and that the presence of residual oxygen did not
represent a significant metabolic advantage. Furthermore,
ethanol, being an easily assimilated substrate, tends to direct
metabolism towards rapid fermentative and acetogenic path-
ways, reducing the residence time of aromatic intermediates
derived from LAS and, therefore, limiting the potential benefit
of microaeration in the partial oxidation of these com-
pounds.39,44
In the presence of sucrose, a pronounced shift was observed
in both the microbial community structure and system
performance. In the microaerated reactor, richness and
diversity indices decreased markedly for both Archaea and
Bacteria, indicating the emergence of a more specialized
community. This pattern is consistent with the fact that
sucrose (hydrolyzed into glucose and fructose) is rapidly
assimilated by bacteria equipped with highly efficient metabolic
machinery for sugar utilization. As these sugars provide a high
energetic yield and enable rapid ATP and biomass production,
microorganisms with higher growth rates tend to outcompete
slower-growing taxa, leading to reductions in diversity and
richness and, in some cases, increased dominance within the
community. Importantly, this community streamlining co-
incided with a substantial increase in LAS removal, particularly
in R2, suggesting that the selective advantage conferred by
sucrose assimilation favored microbial groups potentially
associated with surfactant degradation.
This inverse relationship between diversity and performance
suggests a process of functional selection, in which
microaeration, associated with a more complex substrate
such as sucrose, favored the enrichment of populations
potentially associated with aromatic compound degradation.
Limited oxygenation may have stimulated the activity of
facultative bacteria involved in the initial steps of benzene ring
oxidation, promoting the conversion of recalcitrant intermedi-
ates into molecules more assimilable by subsequent anaerobes,
as already observed by other authors.45,46 Thus, the reduction
in diversity reflected a more targeted and functionally efficient
community, adapted to the degradation of LAS under
controlled microaeration conditions.
In the microaerated reactor, this gradient may have
intensified, creating complementary niches between micro-
aerobic and anaerobic zones, which favor syntrophic pathways
between partial oxidants and residual sulfate or nitrate
reducers, as well as oxygen-tolerant methanogens. Thus, the
greater removal of LAS observed in R2 with sucrose results not
only from the presence of oxygen, but also from the interaction
between the type of co-substrate and the consequent
restructuring of the microbial community towards a more
specialized and synergistic consortium.
The Venn diagram analysis corroborated the diversity
patterns observed in the richness and diversity indices (Figure
4). R1 operated with sucrose exhibited the highest number of
unique ASVs (1762), indicating a more heterogeneous
microbial community under strictly anaerobic conditions. In
contrast, R2 with sucrose presented only 91 unique ASVs and
no ASVs shared with the inoculum, reflecting a strong
microbial selection driven by microaeration and complete
community restructuring. This specialized community co-
incided with the highest LAS removal observed in the study.
Moreover, the presence of only 16 ASVs shared between the
inoculum and all reactors indicates that both co-substrate type
and microaeration acted as major selective forces shaping the
microbial community. Overall, ethanol maintained more
similar communities, whereas sucrose under microaeration
promoted a less diverse but functionally more specialized
consortium.

3.4.4.6. Impact of Microaeration and Co-substrate on LAS
Metabolic Pathways. To integrate the microbiological and
functional findings obtained throughout this study, the
combined effects of microaeration and co-substrate on the
predicted LAS degradation pathways are discussed below. The
results indicate that the influence of microaeration on LAS
degradation was strongly associated with the metabolic
environment established by the co-substrate. Although oxygen
supplementation was applied under the same operational
conditions, its effects differed substantially between ethanol-
and sucrose-fed reactors, suggesting that the response to
microaeration was governed not only by oxygen availability but
also by the structure and functionality of the microbial
consortium supported by each carbon source.
Under ethanol supplementation, LAS degradation appeared
to be primarily driven by conventional anaerobic processes.
The predominance of fermentative and methanogenic micro-
organisms, together with the enrichment of pathways
associated with carbon fermentation and methane production,
suggests that most of the electron flow was likely directed
toward the conversion of readily biodegradable substrates.
Consequently, microaeration produced only limited changes in
LAS removal, indicating that the oxygen supplied was
insufficient to substantially redirect the dominant metabolic
routes established in the reactor.
In contrast, sucrose supplementation resulted in a markedly
different metabolic response. The greater availability of
fermentative intermediates likely created conditions that
favored syntrophic interactions and increased metabolic
flexibility, allowing the microbial community to more
effectively exploit the oxygen introduced through microaera-
tion. This shift was accompanied by the enrichment of
predicted functional pathways potentially associated with
aromatic compound transformation, side-chain oxidation,
sulfur metabolism, and the subsequent conversion of
degradation intermediates. Collectively, these predictions are
consistent with a greater potential for LAS transformation and
further processing of its degradation products.
These findings suggest that microaeration may not have
simply increased the availability of an additional electron
acceptor, but may also have influenced the sequence of
metabolic reactions potentially involved in LAS degradation.
Under sucrose supplementation, oxygen may have facilitated
the initial activation of the surfactant molecule and the
transformation of aromatic intermediates that are typically
degraded slowly under strictly anaerobic conditions. The
resulting intermediates could subsequently be utilized by
anaerobic microorganisms through pathways potentially
involving β-oxidation, sulfur transformation, and methano-
genesis, thereby establishing a complementary interaction
between oxidative and reductive processes.
Therefore, the combined application of microaeration and
sucrose appears to have favored a hybrid degradation pathway
in which oxygen-dependent reactions may have enhanced the
initial transformation of LAS, while anaerobic metabolism
likely contributed to the subsequent conversion of inter-
mediates. This metabolic coupling provides a plausible
mechanistic explanation for the superior LAS removal
observed in the microaerated sucrose-fed reactor and high-
lights the importance of simultaneously considering redox
conditions and co-substrate selection when designing strategies
to improve surfactant removal in anaerobic wastewater
treatment systems.

4. CONCLUSIONS
This study demonstrated the potential of microaeration as a
strategy to improve LAS degradation under anaerobic
conditions. However, the response to oxygen supplementation
differed according to the co-substrate employed, suggesting
that the metabolic environment established within the reactor
may influence the extent to which microaeration stimulates
surfactant transformation. In this regard, the most pronounced
improvement in LAS removal was observed when sucrose was
used as the co-substrate.
The enhanced performance achieved under sucrose
supplementation was associated with a substantial restructuring
of the microbial community and its metabolic functions.
Microaeration favored the establishment of a more specialized
consortium capable of coupling oxidative and anaerobic
degradation pathways, thereby facilitating the conversion of
aromatic and sulfonated intermediates while preserving the
overall functionality of the anaerobic process. These findings
suggest that the benefits of microaeration extend beyond direct
oxygen supply and are closely linked to its ability to reshape
microbial metabolism and promote complementary degrada-
tion routes.
From a practical standpoint, the results suggest that
microaeration can be implemented as a low-cost process
intensification strategy to improve LAS removal in UASB
reactors treating domestic wastewater. The positive response
observed under sucrose supplementation indicates that oxygen
supply and co-substrate selection may act synergistically to
overcome metabolic limitations associated with anaerobic LAS
degradation. Because the improvement was achieved under an
HRT typical of full-scale UASB reactors, the proposed
approach may represent a feasible alternative for enhancing
surfactant removal in existing treatment plants without
substantial infrastructural modifications. Future studies should
investigate the effects of different microaeration rates, redox
mediator supplementation, alternative electron acceptors such
as nitrate and nitrite, evaluate the integration of bioaugmenta-
tion or co-metabolic strategies, and assess the long-term
impacts of microaeration on effluent quality under real-scale
operating conditions.
